ai-ml-evidence-confusion-matrix.essentialQuestion: What do binary confusion-matrix cells count, and when is precision undefined?
ai-ml-evidence-confusion-matrix.verifiedBoundary: At a fixed threshold, TP, FP, FN, and TN partition every labeled binary observation; precision=TP/(TP+FP) and recall=TP/(TP+FN) when denominators are positive.
ai-ml-evidence-confusion-matrix.analogy: Sort ten specimens into four mutually exclusive trays: correct positives, false alarms, missed positives and correct negatives. Ratios only make sense after the trays have exact labels.

starter.plainStart: Treat positive=1 as the event to find. A false positive is a 0 called 1, not just any error.

technical.scope: Only binary labels 0/1, equal-weight observations, declared positive class 1, one decision threshold; ratios are dimensionless.

Predicting no positives makes TP+FP=0: precision is undefined mathematically, not proof of zero false-positive risk; software APIs may assign a configured zero.

ai-ml-evidence-majority-class-baseline.essentialQuestion: Why is 95% accuracy insufficient evidence for detecting a rare positive class?
ai-ml-evidence-majority-class-baseline.verifiedBoundary: A classifier that always predicts the majority class can have high accuracy while zero positive recall; balanced accuracy averages sensitivity and specificity.
ai-ml-evidence-majority-class-baseline.analogy: A detector announcing 'quiet' on every minute can sound 95% successful in a mostly quiet environment while never detecting one alarm.

ai-ml-evidence-threshold-cost-selection.essentialQuestion: How can an operating threshold minimize a declared asymmetric error cost?
ai-ml-evidence-threshold-cost-selection.verifiedBoundary: Given fixed scores, labels and nonnegative false-positive and false-negative costs, empirical decision cost at threshold t is C_FP*FP(t)+C_FN*FN(t); threshold choice depends on costs, not accuracy alone. For fixed distinct observed scores, an optimal empirical cutoff can be found by enumerating the decision changes at sorted score boundaries, including the all-negative case; this is not proof of deployment generalization.
ai-ml-evidence-threshold-cost-selection.analogy: A false alarm costs one inspection, but a missed failure costs four inspections. Moving the alarm threshold changes which kind of cost you pay.

starter.plainStart: A model outputs a score; business loss is defined by explicit actions and asymmetric error penalties, not the score itself.
starter.tryThis: Enumerate each distinct-score cutoff and the all-negative case, then change C_FN from 4 to 0.1; compare the global minimizer, not just two cutoffs.
starter.helper: Enumerate every distinct-score cutoff and the all-negative rule; keep error costs and equality semantics explicit.

technical.scope: Illustrative validation-set cost only, equal cost units per error, and fixed, distinct scores; one score equals the tested threshold 0.3, so the declared positive decision uses p >= t. Choose the threshold on validation data, never on final test labels.
technical.versionCaution: The mathematics in this fixture is version-independent; check the cited library documentation for evolving API behavior.

reasoningSteps: Sort the six distinct scores descending and enumerate inclusive cutoffs t=[Infinity,0.9,0.6,0.55,0.4,0.3,0.2]. With C_FP=1 and C_FN=4, their empirical costs are [12,8,4,5,6,2,3], proving 0.3 is optimal among all possible decision sets at these fixed scores. Any threshold between adjacent observed scores yields an already enumerated decision set.
The equality boundary is observable: y[4]=1 and p[4]=0.3. At t=0.3, p>=t includes this true positive (FP=2, FN=0, cost=2), whereas p>t omits it (FP=2, FN=1, cost=6). State tie semantics explicitly.
A blanket claim that increasing threshold always reduces total cost fails: raising .3 to .5 reduces FP by 1 but raises FN by 1 and cost by 3.

When C_FN falls to 0.1, the same cutoffs cost [0.3,0.2,0.1,1.1,2.1,2,3]; t=0.6 now minimizes empirical cost at 0.1. Selecting or reporting this winner on final test labels would be invalid model selection.

ai-ml-evidence-average-precision-ranking.essentialQuestion: Why does non-interpolated average precision depend on the rank of positive examples?
ai-ml-evidence-average-precision-ranking.verifiedBoundary: For distinct descending scores, binary average precision equals the mean precision-at-rank taken at each positive item, i.e. sum over recall increases P_k*DeltaRecall_k.
ai-ml-evidence-average-precision-ranking.analogy: A reviewer sees ranked search results one at a time. Precision is rewarded at the ranks where a relevant result actually appears.

starter.plainStart: Average precision aggregates precision at successive recovered positives, not just whether all positives can eventually be found.

starter.helper: At each positive rank, compute the cumulative relevant count divided by rank and weight by the change in recall.

technical.scope: Two positives, descending distinct scores, no sample weights or ties; AP is dimensionless and prevalence-sensitive.
technical.versionCaution: The mathematics in this fixture is version-independent; check the cited library documentation for evolving API behavior.

reasoningSteps: Sort scores [.9,.8,.7,.1] with labels [1,0,1,0]. The positives occur at ranks 1 and 3; their precisions are 1/1 and 2/3, hence AP=(1+2/3)/2=5/6≈0.833333.
AP=sum_k precision(k)*DeltaRecall(k). With two positives, each positive produces a recall increment 1/2, so the score equals (1/1)*(1/2)+(2/3)*(1/2)=5/6. Negatives contribute no recall increment.
Treating AP as trapezoidal area under a linearly interpolated PR curve is not generally equivalent; the stepwise precision weighting here is explicit.

ai-ml-evidence-brier-probability-score.essentialQuestion: How does a proper quadratic score penalize confident incorrect probabilities?
ai-ml-evidence-brier-probability-score.verifiedBoundary: Binary Brier score is the arithmetic mean of (p_i-y_i)^2 for probability p in [0,1] and outcome y in {0,1}; lower is better, zero means exact predictions on the observations.
ai-ml-evidence-brier-probability-score.analogy: Two weather forecasts can both say 'rain' under a 50% rule, yet one can deserve a larger penalty for being much more confident when wrong.

ai-ml-evidence-calibration-bin-ece.essentialQuestion: How does bin-level expected calibration error differ from accuracy?

ai-ml-evidence-calibration-bin-ece.analogy: For a tray of cards forecast at 60–90% chance, compare the average stated chance with the fraction actually observed, not a count of classification mistakes.

ai-ml-evidence-preprocessing-leakage.essentialQuestion: How can test-set features leak into a fitted preprocessing statistic?
ai-ml-evidence-preprocessing-leakage.verifiedBoundary: A learned transform must fit only on training observations; including held-out test values changes the fitted statistic and can contaminate model-selection evidence.
ai-ml-evidence-preprocessing-leakage.analogy: Using the final exam scores to decide how to scale study-time scores is already peeking at the held-out exam, even without looking at the right answers.

starter.plainStart: Fitted transforms learn numbers from data; held-out feature values must not enter that learning step in an unbiased holdout evaluation.
starter.tryThis: Compute the mean from training only and freeze it, then apply to held-out data; repeat using a pooled mean solely to falsify the unsafe method.
starter.helper: Split first, fit the centering statistic only on training observations, then apply the frozen statistic to validation and test observations.

technical.scope: One-dimensional synthetic data in arbitrary feature units; simple mean centering, not standard deviation scaling; a pedagogical leakage witness not a measured model-accuracy estimate.
technical.versionCaution: The mathematics in this fixture is version-independent; check the cited library documentation for evolving API behavior.

reasoningSteps: Train x=[0,2] has centering mean 1, so held-out x=10 transforms to 10-1=9. Illegally fitting the mean on [0,2,10] yields mean 4 and transformed test 10-4=6.

The training-only mean is (0+2)/2=1, while the forbidden pooled mean is (0+2+10)/3=4. Fitting the second statistic depends on test features, so it leaks across the holdout boundary even if test labels remain unknown.
Claiming the test labels are never read so leakage is impossible fails: using test features in fitted statistics is still test-set leakage in this workflow.

ai-ml-evidence-stable-binary-logit-loss.essentialQuestion: Why is direct exp(-z) computation unsafe for extreme logits?
ai-ml-evidence-stable-binary-logit-loss.verifiedBoundary: For binary target y in {0,1}, BCE-with-logits equals softplus(z)-y*z, with stable implementation max(z,0)-y*z+log(1+exp(-abs(z))); a sigmoid then log can overflow or underflow.
ai-ml-evidence-stable-binary-logit-loss.analogy: Tracking a bank balance by subtracting two astronomical amounts can lose precision; stable log-sum-exp rearrangement avoids creating enormous intermediate values.

starter.helper: Transform the expression to stable softplus first; no exponential term should have a positive large-magnitude argument.

technical.scope: Unweighted binary targets, natural logarithms, sample mean reduction, logits dimensionless; this is a scalar pedagogical reproduction of a standard loss, not a PyTorch benchmark.

BCE(z,y)=softplus(z)-y*z. Using softplus(z)=max(z,0)+log1p(exp(-abs(z))) eliminates exp of a large positive number while retaining the exact finite-logit objective for y in [0,1].

At z=-1000, a naive sigmoid followed by a logarithm can overflow exp(1000) or evaluate log(0). Stable softplus remains finite: the y=1 loss is 1000 in this numerical example, while the mathematically positive y=0 loss rounds to 0 because exp(-1000) underflows in binary64 floating-point.

ai-ml-evidence-logistic-gradient-update.essentialQuestion: How does one supervised logistic-loss gradient step change a model prediction?
ai-ml-evidence-logistic-gradient-update.verifiedBoundary: For one feature x and scalar weight w with no intercept, p=sigmoid(w*x), d BCE/dw=(p-y)*x. Gradient descent takes w_new=w-alpha*dL/dw.

ai-ml-evidence-ridge-regularized-paramet.essentialQuestion: How does an L2 penalty move an optimum in a one-parameter regression objective?
ai-ml-evidence-ridge-regularized-paramet.verifiedBoundary: For a toy objective J(w)=(w-3)^2+lambda*w^2 with lambda>=0, J'(w)=2(w-3)+2lambda*w; its unique minimizer is w*=3/(1+lambda) when lambda is finite.
ai-ml-evidence-ridge-regularized-paramet.analogy: A spring pulls the best-fit weight toward zero; the optimum balances matching the target against the spring's penalty.

starter.plainStart: An L2 penalty adds a smooth quadratic cost that usually shrinks a coefficient but does not set it exactly to zero.
starter.tryThis: Implement J(w), compare the computed minimizer to two alternative weights and verify derivative near zero using central differences.
starter.helper: Derive the stationary point and verify strict convexity through the second derivative rather than relying on a solver-specific optimizer.

technical.scope: Scalar toy regression, explicitly stated penalty convention (no 1/2 factor), lambda=1 dimensionless; not the exact scaling convention of any particular library.
technical.versionCaution: The mathematics in this fixture is version-independent; check the cited library documentation for evolving API behavior.

reasoningSteps: Set lambda=1, so 2(w-3)+2w=0 gives w*=1.5. J(1.5)=2.25+2.25=4.5; J(3)=0+9=9; unpenalized lambda=0 would choose w=3.
J'(w)=2(w-3)+2lambda*w and J''(w)=2(1+lambda)>0 for lambda>=0. Setting J'=0 therefore yields a unique global minimizer w*=3/(1+lambda), or 1.5 at lambda=1.
'L2 always produces a sparse zero weight' is false here: lambda=1 gives 1.5 rather than zero; sparsity is not the mechanism of L2 shrinkage.

ai-ml-evidence-kmeans-one-lloyd-update.essentialQuestion: Why can an assignment-plus-centroid-update reduce k-means inertia?
ai-ml-evidence-kmeans-one-lloyd-update.verifiedBoundary: For Euclidean 1D k-means with fixed assignments, each cluster's arithmetic mean minimizes its within-cluster squared error; Lloyd's assignment and update steps do not increase inertia under well-defined nonempty clusters.
ai-ml-evidence-kmeans-one-lloyd-update.analogy: Two gathering locations move to the average home of their assigned attendees, reducing their total squared travel distance for those assignments.

starter.plainStart: Lloyd's centroid update chooses the mean of each fixed assigned group because that minimizes the group's squared Euclidean error.
starter.tryThis: Assign each 1D point to the nearest center, calculate both centroid means and old/new inertia; intentionally use one center and observe the different objective.
starter.helper: Optimize cluster means for fixed assignments, then separately reassess assignments; do not equate conditional minimization with global clustering optimality.

technical.scope: Euclidean one-dimensional data in arbitrary units; squared distance units; two nonempty clusters; no ties in this fixture, no stochastic restarts.
technical.versionCaution: The mathematics in this fixture is version-independent; check the cited library documentation for evolving API behavior.

reasoningSteps: Data x=[0,1,8,9], centers initially [0,8] give nearest-cluster assignments [0,0,1,1], inertia 0+1+0+1=2. Updating centers to means [.5,8.5] gives inertia 4*(.5^2)=1.

For n fixed assigned points, the derivative of sum_i(x_i-mu)^2 is 2n*mu-2sum_i x_i. The within-cluster minimizer is the mean, 0.5 for [0,1] and 8.5 for [8,9], lowering fixed-assignment inertia from 2 to 1.

Lloyd updates are not global-optimum certificates. On x=[0,1,5,6,10,12] with k=2, centers [0.5,8.25] yield stable nearest-center groups [0,1] and [5,6,10,12], whose means remain [0.5,8.25] and whose total squared inertia is 33.25. A different stable grouping [0,1,5,6] and [10,12] has centers [3,11] and lower inertia 28.

ai-ml-evidence-prevalence-and-precision-.essentialQuestion: Why can predictive precision change when class prevalence changes but sensitivity and specificity do not?
ai-ml-evidence-prevalence-and-precision-.verifiedBoundary: Bayes' rule gives PPV=(TPR*pi)/(TPR*pi+FPR*(1-pi)); changing positive prevalence pi alone changes precision even with fixed conditional true-positive and false-positive rates.
ai-ml-evidence-prevalence-and-precision-.analogy: A screening test with unchanged sensitivity and false-alarm rate can generate a different share of trustworthy alerts when the event becomes rare.

starter.plainStart: Positive predictive value depends on the prior event rate as well as a classifier's true-positive and false-positive rates.
starter.tryThis: Compute Bayes PPV for two prevalence values, then check the edge case pi=0 with FPR>0 (PPV zero, assuming positive predictions are possible).
starter.helper: Use Bayes' rule to compute true- and false-positive alert shares of the entire population before conditioning on alerts.

technical.scope: Population-level probabilities, binary conditionals held fixed for the thought experiment, no distribution shift in class-conditional score distributions; model probabilities need not be calibrated.
technical.versionCaution: The mathematics in this fixture is version-independent; check the cited library documentation for evolving API behavior.

reasoningSteps: At TPR=.8 and FPR=.1, prevalence pi=.1 gives PPV=.08/(.08+.09)=8/17≈.470588; prevalence pi=.5 gives PPV=.4/(.4+.05)=8/9≈.888889.
Bayes' rule yields PPV=TPR*pi/[TPR*pi+FPR*(1-pi)]. For pi=0.1, true-positive alerts occupy 0.8*0.1=0.08 of the population and false-positive alerts occupy 0.1*0.9=0.09; PPV=8/17.
'Precision is an intrinsic constant of the classifier across deployment populations' is false under a prevalence shift with otherwise fixed rates.
